doc.title: Bill Dobbins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rochester, New York, January 11, 2012

title: Fischer's dominant seventh devices and Shostakovich
summary: Using a major seventh as nonharmonic tone on dominants, the tritone relation, and Shostakovich's First Symphony.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: So one of the things that he uses is in dominant seventh cords, like if you were in B flat 7 going to E flat, if you have a B flat altered chord with a raised ninth in the melody [plays piano] it will result in E flat. Some of the other things he does sometimes is instead of starting directly with a dominant seventh [plays piano] he’ll use the major seventh. It’s a nonharmonic tone. And what that relates to in terms of bebop music is the tritone in there. Because the note that makes the four-three suspension in an E 7 chord, A to G#, in the tritone the B flat 7 in that same line is the major seventh to the minor seventh [plays piano]. So when you play this on an E 7 chord it sounds perfectly — everybody does that. But instead of E 7 going to A, if it’s B flat 7 going to E flat, you use the same upper voices.

Yeah. Some of this is also in Shostakovich’s First Symphony where he does a lot of things where he has a flat 9 in the melody and he not only uses that major 7th, but uses the lowered 5th next to the 3rd. So you get this major second inside too.
